prize_parts.citation: For visionary, densely patterned Romanian prose, rooted in his poetry, that builds memory, the body and dream into an expansive metaphysical project.

statement.case_for: My preferred writer is unchanged from round 1. What changed is the citation wording, narrowed after the chair's scope question. Cărtărescu's voice is unmistakable, and his case on the common criteria is the most complete on the shortlist. The prose is built from long, patterned sentences and recurring images of the body, memory and cosmos. As publicly described, the Blinding (Orbitor) trilogy and Solenoid carry formal ambition at the scale of whole architectures, which is a harder test than a single well-made book. The imaginative and intellectual depth comes from the work's own construction and does not depend on topicality, nationality or political symbolism. On the chair's scope question, I now propose that the citation rest on the prose and name the poetry as formative ground. Translation coverage of the poetry and early work is thin, and I cannot assess it independently. A citation claiming equal weight for poetry would assert more than the evidence in front of me supports. I treat the agreement among the six round-1 files as no evidence of merit. I tested the case again against the stated reservations and the closest alternatives, and it still holds on literary grounds. These judgments rest on public knowledge and the supplied descriptions. I have not independently verified any text.
statement.case_against: The reservation that decides how firmly I hold this view is the unresolved pattern-versus-overextension question. I argued in round 1 that recurring images give the long novels structural logic, and I still read them that way. That is an inference from public descriptions, and I cannot confirm it without close reading of the whole corpus. In answer to the chair's first question, I cannot name the weakest volume with authority. I can only say the strongest evidence is the large architectures. Nothing available to me, such as expert commentary on the Romanian original, shows whether the sentence-level achievement survives translation. The poetry and early prose are thinly covered. A recommendation therefore rests mainly on the late large novels, and the whole-oeuvre claim is only partly tested. The 'idealistic tendency' clause also does not discriminate cleanly in his favour. I read it as open for every candidate and will not use it as a tiebreaker.

responses.point: Olsson now places Cărtărescu first and Carson second. He proposes resting any Carson citation on her written lyric and essay work, with visual form as support. He also concedes that the classical frame may narrow her range.
responses.response: I think his proposal to rest a Carson citation on the written lyric and essay work is the right way to handle the book-object problem. It makes the case stronger than I credited in round 1, because it moves the argument away from Nox as a physical object. It also narrows the claim, as he says, and the question then becomes whether that written corpus shows sustained quality across decades. From public knowledge I can point to the verse novel and the elegiac work as achievements. I cannot show that they sit on a broad, even body of work. For that reason Carson stays my first alternative and I do not move her above Cărtărescu. I still hold, as I said in round 1, that if the committee judged by the best individual books, she would be much closer. I would not oppose her. On the 'idealistic tendency', I agree with Mattson and Sward that the clause does not clearly separate the two.

responses.point: Mattson treats the question of whether the density of the later novels is purposeful pattern or overextension as the main open test. She also argues that every other candidate faces a comparable limit of translation or compactness, and that length is not automatically a virtue.
responses.response: I accept her last point and want to guard against it in my own reasoning: scale is not merit, and I do not claim it is. What I claim is narrower. The recurring images and obsessions return across the long books in a way that reads as construction and not accumulation, and that is an inference from public description. Her argument that translation limits apply to all candidates is fair, but they differ in kind. Carson's difficulty lies partly in material form. Wright's lies in the Aboriginal English and oral registers. Cărtărescu's lies in Romanian rhythm and syntax. None of them is eliminated by this, but I weigh the sentence-carried case as less exposed than the book-object case. That is a judgment of degree, and I hold it with the uncertainty she names. I agree the citation should name the project and not require every volume to be equal.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg says the supplied evidence does not settle whether the late Cărtărescu novels extend the early project or partly repeat it. He keeps Murnane and Michon as alternatives and credits Murnane's austere, self-questioning syntax.
responses.response: His point on extension versus repetition is the one I have least ability to answer, and I would be misleading the committee if I treated my round-1 phrase 'extend the project in scale' as established. It is the reading public descriptions support, and I hold it provisionally. This is also why I narrowed my citation: the wording should claim only the sustained project across the large prose works. On Murnane, I respect the formal discipline and the self-questioning syntax. My hesitation remains that a deliberately closed method gives less evidence of development across a body of work. He has said himself that breadth of significance is uncertain, and I do not take the narrowness as a defect. If someone can show variation of register or development in the later books, that would raise him in my view, but that is not an argument I currently have.

responses.point: Carlberg holds Wright as an alternative and not her preference. She argues that the citation should rest on the invention of the novel's form, and she doubts that the small number of major novels gives enough evidence of sustained quality.
responses.response: We are close here. I agree that a Wright citation would have to rest on form and invented idiom, with the Indigenous-sovereignty theme realised through that form and not substituting for it. Her point about the number of major works is the same one I made in round 1, and I have not found an answer to it. In response to the chair's question about what would move Wright from alternative to preferred, my answer is further major work, or a closer reading of the oral and idiomatic registers than I can offer through English. Neither is the fault of the writing. The obstacle is volume and my reading, not quality. I would add one caution. Time-in-career should not become a reason for the committee to hold back a case that is already strong in kind, but I do not think Wright's case outweighs Cărtărescu's on the whole-oeuvre criterion today.

responses.point: Sward proposes anchoring the citation in the prose and mentioning poetry cautiously. She says her round-1 exchange with me moved her toward treating Wright as a closer alternative.
responses.response: Her proposal is the closest to where I have ended up, and her caution about the thin poetry coverage is better stated than mine was in round 1. I now propose prose as the object of the citation and poetry as its formative ground. This resolves the dispute over poetry's weight without asserting something none of us can assess in the original. I am glad the Wright discussion was useful to her. Her own view that the evidence for a deepening vision across a long career is stronger for Cărtărescu matches my ordering, and I would not ask her to move him down. I would only ask that Wright's case be judged on its form, as she says, and that the shortlist not treat her smaller corpus as a judgment on the ambition of the novels.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's rhythm, syntax and sonic patterning survives in translation. I cannot name expert commentary on the Romanian original, and I have not read the Romanian.
Whether the very long late novels extend the early project or partly repeat it, and which volumes are strongest and weakest. This needs close reading of the whole corpus, which I have not done.
The poetry and early prose are thinly covered in translation. That is why I narrowed the citation to prose with poetry as formative ground; the whole-oeuvre claim is only partly tested.
For Carson, how much of the written lyric and essay corpus carries sustained quality once the book-objects and translations are set aside as supporting material.
For Wright, whether a small number of very large novels is enough for the sustained-quality criterion, and how well I can read the oral and idiomatic registers through English.
How Nobel's 'idealistic tendency' applies to any candidate. I see it as open and non-discriminating, and I have not independently verified any source.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile as regards any shortlisted writer. My own literary practice and my work on Selma Lagerlöf are context only. The profile records co-election with David Håkansson in 2023 and a collaboration with Kate Larson. Neither is a documented tie to a shortlisted writer, and I do not treat them as grounds for recusal. The profile also notes that my 2024 Nobel interview was given for the committee and does not establish a personal preference. I disclose these facts without adjudicating them. Why I was co-opted in 2024 and made a full member in 2025 is not documented.
